translator: Claude (AI), draft, not reviewed by a Hittitologist
intro: A New Script anthology tablet of rituals against plague, joined from six fragments. It opens with the broken end of a ritual involving augurs, closed by an internal colophon (§0–4). Then come the army-camp rituals of the augurs Maddunani of Arzawa (§5–8) and Dandanku (§9–14), which duplicate KUB 7.54, and finally the ritual of Zarpiya of Kizzuwatna against plague in the land, which begins in the last lines of §14, runs to §27 and duplicates KBo 13.212+.

paras.en: […] the augur […] in […] […] […] in the city […] […] […] they throw […] […] […] [— gap of unknown length —] […] then […]
[…] they hold […]; and the ḫarša-(?) he scatters(?) away […] he cuts off […] he speaks:

[…] they go to an untouched place. […] and the tongues three times […] the tongues … from one (side?), leafy branches(?) […] … a clay figure on the ground […] they turn […] […] in […] [— gap —] […] … […] …
[…] after the offering […] […] to Zitḫariya (and) the [Mother-god]dess(?) he libates. One jug of beer, one b[owl …], two GÚG-breads, one sweet bread; for a puppy […]; five PURSĪTU-bowls.
[Colophon:] One long tablet, complete. […] the augurs […] … […] Or if […] the king […]

Thus (says) Madu[nan]i, the augur, man of [Arzawa]: [If] a pl[ague] breaks out in the army camp, (and) horses (and) cattle [are dying] terribly(?), [then] they [perform] the mūra[nza]-ritual (meaning unclear). [They perform it as fol]lows: two puppies, one pi[glet …] [… ḫul]liti- (?), fourteen bread [balls …] […] six cups, one [set …] […]. I take all this. […] I prepare (it). […] and the old man […] a puppy […] […] they carry […], and meanwhile [they speak as follows]: '[…] if […] ev[il] […]' [— gap of about five lines —] […] […] and the cups […] […] he speaks […]: '[…] and (it is) for you to eat […]' […] and the full cups […] they come away.
[…] then they take […] […] and these […] […] and a pup[py …] […] these […] […] […]
When they perform the ritual […] […], they take (as an omen) a favourable (bird) coming […]; and when […] they complete (it), then [they take] a bird [coming] behind […].
This ritual the old man, together with the augur, set about performing.

[Thus (says)] Dandanku, the augur: If […] [there is dy]ing(?), this ritual […] […] [fodder mixt]ure […] mixed in(?), grain, straw, red wool, […] green wool […] they take; and grain (and) straw [they mix together …] […] across [the ḫadda]ri- [of the road] (crossroads?) […], and he speaks as follows: 'The grooms [who are] yours, (those) of the god Iyarri: let them give this fodder mixture to the horses! And let the maidservants of the god take the blue wool, red wool, green wool, black wool and white wool!'

Afterwards he takes one kid, one piglet and one puppy, and they cut them apart for the [Sebettu] (the 'Seven') in an untouched place, across (the way). Afterwards he libates beer (and) wine, each three times, to the Sebettu. Then they come away. The first day is complete.
On the second day they do exactly the same again.

On the third day they perform the ritual, and they take these (things): fourteen thick loaves of a tarna-measure of emmer flour, one cheese, one sour (loaf), three warm loaves, one sweet bread, one GÚG-bread, one jug of beer, one bowl of [wine], one bronze cup, one dagger, two billy goats, one puppy, one quiver — and in it thirty arrows —, one bow, one donkey, six cups, two GÌR.GÁN-vessels, one jug of water, two pots. When he has prepared all this,

the ritual patron goes to the open country, and they carry the ritual (materials) to the open country too. On this side and on that side […] they […]. One billy goat [and one pupp]y for […] they cut apart […]; they lift […] away […]; they come […] place […] warp[a-] (enclosure?) […] [— several broken lines —] […] […] [Iya]rri, the Sebettu […] to Iyarri […] … to those very (gods?) […] the …s (and) the heart he c[ooks] on the fire, and each (portion) he places before the gods. Then […] … he libates three times. Then the ritual patron […] to ea[t(?) …] […] [one(?)] billy goat, sweet bread (and) GÚG-bread he places for Iyarri […]. They bring the meat, and the leg […] they […]. They eat, and the ritual patron [begins(?)] to drink […]: he drinks (to) Iyarri three times […]. The gods of Iyarri, marwainzi (meaning unclear), […]. And afterwards again (he drinks to) Iyarri once […]. 'And afterwards the maidservants, the staff-bearers, the c[ooks …]' — he drinks three times. When […] to eat […], the ritual patron steps up, and a donkey [they drive up]. But if (he is) a poor man, they make a donkey of clay […]. They turn (its) eyes towards the enemy land, and [they speak] th[us]: 'You, Iyarri, [have done evil] to th[is land …]; now [let this donkey lift it up and] carry (it) [into the enemy land]!' […] […] the arrows […]: 'O [god], the land [of the enemy …]! But when [you come] into the land of [Ḫatti], let (your quiver) be closed; and the bow […]' […] away […]

On the fourth day, when it grows light, […] of a tarna-measure, two warm loaves, […] GÚG-bread […], one ḫanešša-jug […] they carry, and for each […]. And three roads likewise […] … to […]. And at each (place) three thick loaves […]; and at each (place), for one road, […] to the god […] he libates. They cut up the billy goats, and which […] the skin he fixes on top of a pole(?); their heads, however, […] right inside the skin. The fat they cook entirely; the […] (and) the heart they cook on the fire, and of each the li[ver …] he places in front of it. Beer (and) wine on the roads […] he libates, and he says: 'O god, see, for you […] we have fixed up(?) a billy goat; and when(?) you come […] […] let him take […], and to the land of Ḫatti in favour […] […] …, but not again […] […] look with favour on the land of Ḫat[ti] […]!' […] Then the ritual patron […] to eat […] […] and he takes(?) a tasting portion […] for the god […] […] and […] […] Iyarri […] […] the Sebettu […]. [— beginning of the ritual of Zarpiya: —] [If] the year is ruined (i.e. bad) […] […] in whichever city […] […] he performs […]
[…] bronze […] […] its footstool […] […] of lapis lazuli he …s (šišai) […] […] ḫaleešša- (?) […] […] a dog's sinew […] […] one (he hangs) on a peg of medlar(?) wood […] […] he hangs up.
[…] he strikes […] […] … […] and [on th]is side, at the gate, […] […] [a kukkulla-(cake)], cooked, […] [… a jug of wi]ne he hangs up.
[…] … ašara- (wood?) […] […] [na]me(?) […] … [— gap of unknown length —] […] … […]

'[… we have] sworn (an oath), and then […] […] we have drunk. So do not step (again) to my [gate(?)]!' […] and the whole billy goat […]. […] When the fat is done, the liver (and) the heart […] [they br]ing. And beside it […] […] (loaves of) [ha]lf a handful they bring.
[…] the livers (and) the heart he places […], and speaks as follows: 'Above and below […]! […] let the father-gods eat! […] let [them] eat!
[… be] [witness]es!' Then […] […] [the tab]le of the Innara[want-gods] […] […] nine(?) thick lo[aves] […]
[…] … wood […] [— gap of unknown length —] [Luwian incantation, fragmentary, not translated]
[…] he speaks:
[Luwian incantation, fragmentary, not translated]
[Luwian line, fragmentary, not translated]
[…] he closes […] […] he speaks:
'[…] let [it] be held fast(?) inside!'
[Colophon:] […] complete.
